subject: Chemistry
title: The Elephant Toothpaste Reaction
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: The Elephant Toothpaste Reaction.

hook.text: Mix hydrogen peroxide with potassium iodide and dish soap. A giant foam snake erupts from the container.

buildup.text: Hydrogen peroxide slowly decomposes into water and oxygen. The iodide ion speeds this up dramatically.

discovery.text: Soap traps the released oxygen as bubbles, creating a massive foam eruption that looks like toothpaste.

twist.text: It's a catalytic decomposition. The iodide isn't consumed—it speeds the reaction without being used up.

climax.text: The foam is warm to the touch. The reaction is exothermic—it releases heat as peroxide breaks down.

punchline.text: Peroxide, iodide, soap. A foam volcano in seconds. Chemistry's best show.

quiz.question: What role does potassium iodide play in elephant toothpaste?
options: It acts as a catalyst, speeding up hydrogen peroxide decomposition
It changes the color of the reaction

details.summary: Elephant toothpaste is a dramatic demonstration where hydrogen peroxide rapidly decomposes into water and oxygen using potassium iodide as a catalyst, with dish soap trapping the oxygen into a massive foam eruption that resembles toothpaste for an elephant.
details.whyItMatters: This reaction is one of the most popular chemistry demonstrations worldwide because it visually illustrates catalysis, decomposition, and exothermic reactions in an unforgettable way.
takeaways: Potassium iodide catalyzes rapid hydrogen peroxide decomposition
The foam is trapped oxygen gas mixed with soap and water
The reaction demonstrates catalysis in a visually dramatic way

faq.question: Is the elephant toothpaste reaction dangerous to perform?
faq.answer: The standard classroom version using three percent hydrogen peroxide is safe. Professional demonstrations use thirty percent concentration, which can cause chemical burns. Proper safety equipment including gloves and goggles is essential for higher concentrations.

faq.question: Why does adding a catalyst make the reaction so much faster?
faq.answer: Hydrogen peroxide naturally decomposes very slowly. The iodide ions from potassium iodide lower the activation energy dramatically, allowing the decomposition to occur in seconds rather than months without being consumed in the process.
